```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
forks <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive")
cells <- readr::read_csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# fixed decimals and a true minus sign; pct() takes values already in per cent and
# rounds halves up, as the specification menu does, so that the pages agree
num <- \(x, d = 3) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
pct <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(floor(x * 10^d + 0.5) / 10^d, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

ref <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
share_below <- 100 * mean(curve$supports)
share_sig <- 100 * mean(curve$supports & curve$sig)
share_cr1 <- 100 * mean(curve$supports & curve$p_cr1 < 0.05)
share_conv <- 100 * mean(curve$supports & curve$p_conv < 0.05)
n_resp <- sum(cells$n_cy)
fk <- \(ax) forks$share[forks$axis == ax]
# the four decisions that barely move the curve, taken together
minor <- sum(forks$share[forks$axis %in% c("noop", "measure", "pred_form", "cell_weight")])
```

The curve of the claim in this course holds `r nrow(curve)` specifications fitted to the 270 country-years of the EU-frames panel (`data/spec_curve.csv`), every one of them a defensible way of asking whether national unemployment or growth moves the positive framing of the EU, and it forms the backdrop of the class chart on the [Multiverse page](multiverse.qmd). Each point on it is placed by its partial correlation and classed by a test of its own, with errors clustered by country under the CR2 correction and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. This reading explains the inferential logic that governs a design of that kind: why the curve as a whole is reported descriptively, why its points cannot be counted as so many independent tests, why a single formal test of the whole curve can nonetheless be designed, why such a test belongs at the level of the country-year, and how its result would be read. The reasoning is elementary but seldom set out in full, and the vocabulary of 'multiverse' and 'specification curve' is young enough that the two terms are routinely conflated.

## Description and inference {#the-two-jobs-of-the-curve}

A multiverse analysis, in the sense given to the term by Steegen and colleagues, is a descriptive exercise: identify every defensible way of turning raw data into a test of the claim, run all of them, and display the resulting distribution instead of a single hand-picked estimate [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse]. Nothing in that founding formulation involves a joint hypothesis test. The founding paper reports grids of estimates and p-values and asks the reader to see how conclusions shift across the grid, and its contribution is transparency about analytical contingency. The inferential layer arrived later and separately, under the name 'specification curve analysis', when Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson supplemented the descriptive curve with a formal question, whether a curve like this could have arisen from data in which the effect does not exist, and with a resampling method for answering it [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis]. The two layers can be used separately, and the largest robustness exercise yet conducted in the social sciences chose to use only the descriptive one. Multi100 reported the dispersion of its 504 reanalyses in explicitly exploratory terms, with no inferential statistics anywhere in the paper [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness].

This course follows that precedent for the curve as a whole. The curve, the decomposition of its variance by decision and the placement of the five reanalyses and of the original study on it are descriptive throughout, even though every point carries its own test. A single permutation-based test of the whole curve could supplement them, fixed in its design before it runs and confined to the country-year level, and the sections below set out that design. The course has designed the test and has not run it, so what follows is also a guide to reading such a test when you meet one in published work.

## Estimates and tests

The descriptive curve invites vote counting. With `r pct(share_below)` of the specifications below zero, and `r pct(share_sig)` below zero with p < 0.05 under CR2 errors clustered by country, against the 2.5% that chance alone would put there if each specification were a separate test of a true null, the count can look as though it settles the question. It cannot, because the specifications are not independent of one another. All `r nrow(curve)` results come from the same 270 country-years, which are averaged from the same `r format(n_resp, big.mark = ",")` respondents and analysed `r nrow(curve)` times in slightly different ways. If the panel happens, by sampling accident alone, to contain a negative-looking alignment between unemployment and positive framing, then most specifications will detect that same accident together, and the points on the curve rise and fall together because every one of them is fitted to the same data. Even the test that classes them rests every time on the same 27 countries, so that the few countries which dominate one clustered standard error dominate those of its neighbours as well. If unemployment and framing were in fact unrelated (a true null hypothesis), the share of specifications in the significant class would therefore have no known distribution. It could be 10% or 70%, and no formula can say which, because the correlations among hundreds of overlapping specifications cannot be derived mathematically [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis].

Every individual point of the curve still has its own inference, an estimate with a standard error and a p-value, and each of those is as interpretable as it would be in a stand-alone paper. On this curve that inference rests on standard errors clustered by country with the CR2 correction of @BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard, tested on degrees of freedom of the kind that Satterthwaite proposed, in the form that @PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust worked out for clustered errors. Clustering allows the ten years of one country to be correlated with one another, which the conventional standard error does not, and the difference is large: under conventional errors, which treat the 270 country-years as independent, `r pct(share_conv)` of the specifications would lie below zero with p < 0.05, against `r pct(share_sig)` under CR2. The CR2 correction adjusts each clustered standard error for the unequal weight of the countries in the fit, which the standard clustered errors (CR1) ignore.

The degrees of freedom of the test matter as much as its standard error. A clustered standard error is estimated from 27 country totals rather than from 270 cells, and the standard practice tests it on 26 degrees of freedom, one fewer than the number of countries. That count assumes that every country contributes about equally to the estimate, and on this panel they do not: a few countries, Greece and Spain above all, hold a disproportionate share of the variation in unemployment that is left once the fixed effects have been removed, and a clustered standard error then rests on those few countries more than on the rest. The Satterthwaite approximation measures how much independent information a clustered variance of that shape carries, and returns a number of degrees of freedom that falls as the information concentrates in fewer countries. On this curve the number runs from `r num(min(curve$df_cr2), 1)` to `r num(max(curve$df_cr2), 1)`, with a median of `r num(stats::median(curve$df_cr2), 1)`, so that the 27 countries behave like about `r round(stats::median(curve$df_cr2))`. The consequence is a stricter threshold: a t of `r num(stats::qt(0.975, 26), 2)` clears 5% on 26 degrees of freedom, but on `r round(stats::median(curve$df_cr2))` it has to reach `r num(stats::qt(0.975, round(stats::median(curve$df_cr2))), 2)`. Under CR1 errors on 26 degrees of freedom `r pct(share_cr1)` of the specifications would lie below zero with p < 0.05. @ImbensKolesar2016RobustStandardErrors show that tests of this kind keep their stated error rate with few or unbalanced clusters where the standard clustered test does not.

The reproduced specification of Task 3, with its conventional t of `r num(ref$t)` on `r ref$df` degrees of freedom, has a CR2 t of `r num(ref$t_cr2)` on `r num(ref$df_cr2, 1)` Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and a p-value of `r num(ref$p_cr2, 4)`, so that under the rule of the course it lies below zero but, by a narrow margin, is not significant at 5%; under CR1 errors on 26 degrees of freedom the same estimate has p = `r num(ref$p_cr1)`, and under conventional errors p = `r num(ref$p_conv, 4)`. The threshold itself means here what it usually means. Each test draws on 270 country-years, with residual degrees of freedom between `r min(curve$df)` and `r max(curve$df)` in the conventional fit and far fewer once the errors are clustered by the 27 countries, so a coefficient has to be large relative to the variation among countries before it clears 5%, whereas a respondent-level model that treats hundreds of thousands of rows as independent, although they share a predictor that takes only 270 values, makes almost any coefficient significant.

What is missing is a warranted statement about the curve as a whole. The gap matters because analytical flexibility is the mechanism by which false positives are produced. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn's demonstration that undisclosed flexibility "allows presenting anything as significant" is the same arithmetic read in the opposite direction [@SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology]. A multiverse inverts the disclosure problem, putting every fork on display rather than hiding it in a garden of unreported paths [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience], but display alone does not turn a set of correlated results into a body of evidence with known error rates.

## The permutation test

The solution that Simonsohn and colleagues adapted is among the oldest ideas in statistics: if the sampling distribution of a quantity cannot be derived, generate it by rearranging the data so that the null hypothesis is true by construction [@Fisher1935DesignExperiments; @Ernst2004PermutationMethods]. Here the null hypothesis is that national economic performance and EU framing are unrelated, and the rearrangement that makes it true is a within-country permutation of the macroeconomic series. Each country keeps its own ten-year history of unemployment and growth and its own outcome data, but the assignment of those values to years is shuffled, jointly for the two series so that they keep their mutual correlation, and the alignment between economic conditions and framing is thereby destroyed. On each such rearrangement the `r nrow(curve)` specifications of the curve are refitted, each is classed by the same CR2 test, and the curve is summarised by three numbers: the median claim-aligned partial correlation, the share of specifications below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, and an aggregate z following Stouffer's rule, which converts the p-value of each specification into a z score, sums those scores and divides by the square root of their number. Five hundred rearrangements give five hundred versions of what this curve looks like when nothing is going on. The observed curve is set beside them, and its rank in that set is the p-value.

The construction deals with the dependence problem set out in the previous section. Every null draw refits the same specifications on the same panel, so every null curve has the same correlation structure that made the observed curve impossible to test by analytical means, and the dependence is reproduced inside the reference distribution instead of being assumed away. For this reason curve-level permutation has become the standard inferential test for large specification exercises, including well-known applied examples [@OrbenPrzybylski2019AssociationAdolescentWellbeing; @RohrerEtAl2017ProbingBirthOrderEffects]. The two tests answer different questions and do not replace each other. The CR2 test asks whether one specification could have produced its slope by chance, given how the countries vary, and the permutation asks whether the whole curve could have taken its shape by chance.

The test also has limits. The permutation destroys temporal alignment, and with it any year-to-year persistence in the predictor, so the null hypothesis that it builds in is 'no association at any alignment', which a sceptic could note is subtly stronger than 'no causal effect'. Two series that trend together can lead the test to reject such a null without any causal connection between them, which is why the two-way specifications of the curve, which remove the change common to every country in a given year, matter for interpretation. It is also why the result of the test is a statement about alignment beyond chance and never about causation, so the estimand questions of Part 2 still apply however small the p-value.

## The level of the identifying variation {#where-the-identifying-variation-lives}

The design confines this test to the country-year level, and the main reason is substantive. The predictor in this study varies only between country-years: the respondents observed in a given country and year, `r format(n_resp, big.mark = ",")` of them across the panel, share one value of the unemployment rate. All the information in the data about the alignment of unemployment with EU framing therefore comes from 270 pairings, one for each country-year cell, in every specification and at every level of analysis. A multiverse of respondent-level models refitted under each of 500 permutations would test the same 270-cell alignment, since the respondent-level rows are, from the point of view of the null hypothesis, an elaborate disaggregation of the same evidence, and it would do so at several hundred times the computational cost, with the added numerical problems of mixed models fitted by maximum likelihood many thousands of times. Such a multiverse would be worth building as a description, because it would show how the size of standardised effects, and their conversion to a common metric, depend on the unit of analysis, a point that the [individual-level module](../../companion/individual-level.qmd) and the conversion lesson of the [case study](index.qmd#sec-conversion) take up. It would have essentially nothing further to contribute to the question 'is the alignment distinguishable from chance?', because it contains no additional identifying variation with which to answer it.

This is also the reply to an objection that a careful reviewer should raise: that the original study modelled individuals, so a test confined to country-year aggregates excludes the kind of model that the original study itself used. The objection conflates the two layers. The respondent-level designs are represented in the description, where the published coefficient of the original author (OA) and the results of the two reanalysts who modelled respondents are placed on the curve as reference marks, each on the degrees of freedom of its own inference, and the individual-level module fits those designs on their own terms. The permutation layer asks a single question about a single alignment, at the level at which that alignment is observed.

## Reading the five hundred draws {#how-many-draws-and-how-to-read-the-result}

The design fixes five hundred permutations in advance, and the consequences for interpretation are mechanical. A permutation p-value is computed with the observed statistic included in its own reference distribution, Phipson and Smyth's correction, which guarantees that an estimated p can never be exactly zero [@PhipsonSmyth2010PermutationPValues], so with B = 500 the smallest attainable two-sided value is $2/(B + 1)$, roughly 0.004. Monte Carlo error, the random error that comes from using a finite number of permutations, follows the binomial rule: an estimated p near 0.05 has a standard error of about $\sqrt{0.05 \times 0.95 / 500} \approx 0.01$. Both facts bear on how a result should be read. A reported p of 0.03 or 0.08 should be treated as 'near the conventional threshold, with one point of Monte Carlo noise either way'. The CR2 test that classes each point carries no error of this kind, since it is computed in closed form, but its threshold is a convention all the same, and a point lying just above or below 5%, as the reproduced specification does, should not be read as a different finding from its neighbours. The choice of B trades that noise against computation in a way that has been formalised for the bootstrap and applies to the permutation unchanged [@DavidsonMacKinnon2000BootstrapTests]. Had finer resolution been needed, a larger B would be fixed in advance. For a supplementary test whose role is calibration rather than discovery, this resolution is sufficient, and its cost, hours of computation against days for a respondent-level equivalent, is proportionate.

## Without the test

The conclusions of the day are built so that they would lose nothing if the test were never run. Four of them are claims about the composition of analytical variation. The first is the decomposition of the curve, in which the estimator carries `r pct(fk("estimator"))` of the variance of the claim-aligned partial correlations and the predictor `r pct(fk("predictor"))`, while the rule for respondents who mention nothing, the published series, the predictor form and the cell weighting together carry `r pct(minor)`. The second is the placement of the five Multi100 reanalyses and of the original study among the `r nrow(curve)` specifications, the third the set of options that left the curve and what each would do to it, which the [decision map](map.qmd) lays out, and the fourth the reading of the recorded dispersion as, in large part, a product of the conversion to a common scale, and for the rest a multiverse of different questions rather than of different analyses of one question [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial; @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand]. All four are established by listing the specifications and decomposing their variance, with no null distribution involved. The distinction between same-conclusion and same-number robustness is likewise descriptive vocabulary [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. The permutation test would answer one narrow supplementary question, whether a curve this claim-consistent could plausibly arise when nothing is going on. Fixing that test in advance, at the level where its identifying variation is found, with a resolution stated before anything runs and in a form that is cheap to reproduce, would add a calibration that the descriptive layers cannot supply, while the conclusions of the day rest on the layers that need no simulation to be understood [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse; @DelGiudiceGangestad2021TravelersGuideMultiverse].
